summary: Cryonova is a free web app that helps students, teachers and farmers find out whether their local climate is really changing, using live NASA data. A user asks a plain question, for example "Does the change in soil temperature affect crops in Colombia?". The AI assistant turns it into a complete research question: it picks the right variables from 88 live-verified variables, and it chooses the place and the period. Everything stays editable. Cryonova then queries NASA at that moment and shows the trend with its uncertainty, coverage and full provenance. In this example, the ground surface in Colombia is clearly warming (+0.38 °C per decade, 2006–2025), while rainfall and soil moisture show no clear trend yet. This addresses the Earth System Trend Detective challenge by separating real trends from noise, honestly. It matters because NASA data is open, but sound answers still require code and statistics.
details:
What it does Cryonova turns a simple question into a reproducible trend analysis of live NASA data, with no account and no coding.

How it works

  1. Ask or set up. Type a question in plain English, or choose variables, a start and end month, and a country or a custom area on an interactive globe.
    • an annotated main chart;
    • the seasonal cycle, monthly anomalies, seasonal trends, a period comparison and a ranking of years;
    • a trend-comparison table;
    • a caption explaining each chart in plain language.

Example result (live run) Colombia, Jan 2006 – Dec 2025, NASA MERRA-2:

  • Surface skin temperature: +0.38 °C per decade, a clear trend (a +0.73 °C fitted change, 2.3 times the normal year-to-year variation). The coolest month was in December 2010 and the hottest in March 2024.
  • Rainfall and root-zone soil moisture: no clear trend yet.

For a farmer, that means the ground is clearly getting hotter, but the water for plants is not keeping up. Plan for heat. This is a climate signal, not a yield forecast.

Benefits and impact

  • Brings rigorous, reproducible trend analysis to classrooms, farmers and local planners.
  • Honest about uncertainty: it says "no clear trend yet" instead of over-claiming.
  • Works for any place, any variable and any period; the farmer question is just one example.

Data and validation

  • Seven live data sources, all verified live on the app's Data sources page: NASA MERRA-2, GPM IMERG, GLDAS, SeaWiFS and Giovanni (via Harmony), plus Copernicus ERA5 and NOAA Climate Data Online.
  • Provenance: every run records product, version and fetch time.
  • Trend checks: estimates match statsmodels on 24 test cases.
  • Automated tests: 146 unit tests and 18 browser tests, including WCAG AA accessibility checks.

Limits

  • Regions are rectangular boxes, so they include some sea or neighbouring land.
  • Grid cells are about 50 km wide.
  • Results are long-term trends, not forecasts, and show what changed, not why.

Tools

  • Application: TypeScript, Next.js and React on Vercel, with a Neon PostgreSQL database (Drizzle).
  • Charts and maps: Plotly and an orthographic globe built with d3-geo.
  • Data reading: h5wasm for HDF5/NetCDF files.
  • AI: the Anthropic Claude API.
  • Validation and testing: Python (statsmodels, SciPy), Vitest and Playwright, with GitHub Actions for CI.

Source code: https://github.com/MariaAlejandraBoadaRodriguez/cryonova

Creativity A research guide, not just a data viewer. It shows how a simple question becomes a complete one, explains its choices and limits, and never lets the AI invent a number.
